rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread an unknown 10-component mixture across the full window while still eluting strongly retained compounds. This first run should reveal overall retention range, any missing late peaks, and whether selectivity needs to shift with temperature or gradient bounds.

All 10 compounds are already baseline-resolved, so the only room to improve CRF is reducing analysis time. Shortening the gradient while keeping composition range and temperature fixed should pull the last peak earlier; this run will test how much speed we can gain before resolution starts to erode.

The 12 min gradient is fast but compresses the critical middle pair too much, so a small increase in gradient time should restore full resolution with little or no time penalty in the CRF. Keeping phi0, phi1, and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient slope near the current optimum.

The optimum appears very close: 14 min is nearly ideal but the critical pair is still just below 1.5, so a modest further increase in gradient time is the most likely path to CRF 1.000. This directly tests whether a slightly shallower gradient lifts the minimum resolution over the target while keeping runtime short.

Gradient time 14 min is closest to optimal, so the best remaining lever is a small selectivity change to improve the critical 6/7 pair without increasing runtime. Dropping temperature slightly often increases retention and can alter relative spacing enough to push the minimum resolution above 1.5 while keeping the run in the zero time-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity badly, so test the opposite direction at the near-optimal 14 min gradient. A small increase to 45 C may improve the critical mid-cluster separation enough to exceed 1.5 without pushing the run into a time-penalty regime.

Temperature changes worsened selectivity, so keep the near-optimal 14 min and 40 C conditions but lower phi0 to make the early/mid gradient effectively shallower at the column. This may selectively expand the crowded central region and lift the critical pair over 1.5 while keeping all compounds within the no-time-penalty window.

Lowering phi0 did not improve the critical pair, so test the opposite direction to shift selectivity in the crowded middle while preserving the near-optimal gradient time and temperature. A slightly higher starting organic can sometimes open a compressed cluster even if overall retention drops modestly.

Changing phi0 only nudged the critical pair, so now reduce phi1 slightly to make the effective gradient shallower later in the run, where the crowded mid/late cluster likely forms. This keeps the proven 14 min, 40 C framework while probing a different selectivity lever that may lift the 6/7 resolution above 1.5 with minimal time cost.

We already reached CRF 1.000, so this is a nearby robustness probe rather than an optimization necessity. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the perfect score persists with a slightly shallower late gradient, which could confirm a broader optimum around the winning method.

Since 14 min with phi1 0.85 is perfect, the only useful remaining question is whether the same selectivity can be retained at a faster gradient. Shortening to 12 min tests whether the lower phi1 preserves adequate resolution for the critical pair while potentially defining a more efficient robust neighborhood around the optimum.

A 12 min gradient at phi1 0.85 is too steep for the critical pair, so this brackets the optimum on the slower side while staying very close to the perfect condition. Testing 16 min will show whether the CRF maximum at 14 min is sharp or whether there is a broader robust plateau around the winning selectivity.

With the optimum already found, the most informative remaining experiments are local robustness checks around that winning selectivity. Lowering phi0 while keeping phi1 0.85 and tG 14 min tests whether the perfect score depends specifically on the starting composition or persists across a broader operating window.

The lower-phi0 robustness check stayed fully resolved but incurred a small time penalty, so the complementary higher-phi0 check will map the other side of the local optimum. This tests whether the perfect score is centered specifically at phi0 0.10 or whether a higher starting strength can maintain full resolution with slightly shorter retention.

We now have two perfect methods, and the higher phi0 version is slightly faster, so the next useful step is to probe whether this perfect region extends further in that direction. Testing phi0 0.20 with the same phi1, tG, and temperature checks the edge of the robustness plateau while potentially maintaining full resolution and short retention.

phi0 0.15 and phi1 0.85 gave a perfect score, while lowering phi1 at phi0 0.10 increased resolution but added time; combining the stronger start with the shallower late gradient is a logical local robustness test. This checks whether the second perfect method remains optimal or near-optimal when phi1 is reduced one step.

Among the perfect methods, phi0 0.15/phi1 0.85 is slightly faster than phi0 0.10/phi1 0.85, so it is worth testing whether that selectivity tolerates a shorter 12 min gradient. This directly probes whether a still-faster method can remain in the maximum-CRF region or if the optimum truly requires 14 min.

The remaining uncertainty is robustness of the perfect method to temperature, since at phi0 0.10 temperature shifts strongly degraded the critical pair. Testing 45 C with the stronger-start perfect method will show whether this alternative optimum is more temperature-tolerant or similarly narrow.

The perfect method is highly temperature-sensitive upward, so a complementary lower-temperature check will complete the local robustness map around the best condition. This will show whether the optimum is centered sharply at 40 C or whether only higher temperature is problematic.

The optimum region is now well mapped, so a final informative local corner is the stronger-start/shallower-finish combination adjacent to the perfect method. This tests whether the loss seen at phi0 0.20, phi1 0.85 is rescued by lowering phi1, or whether phi0 0.20 is simply beyond the robust optimum boundary.

A third perfect method at phi0 0.20/phi1 0.80 suggests the optimum plateau may extend toward stronger starting conditions. Testing phi0 0.25 with the same phi1, tG, and temperature probes the next edge of that plateau and may identify the highest-starting composition that still maintains CRF 1.000.

phi0 0.20/phi1 0.80 is perfect, while increasing phi0 to 0.25 causes an early coelution, so the next informative boundary test is a slightly lower phi1 at the proven phi0 0.20. This will show whether the perfect plateau extends toward a shallower late gradient without reintroducing early compression.

The perfect region appears to run through phi0 0.15–0.20 and phi1 0.80–0.85, while reducing phi1 at phi0 0.20 remains fully resolved but slower. Testing phi0 0.15/phi1 0.75 maps the adjacent corner of this plateau and checks whether the earlier-starting perfect method also tolerates a lower final organic strength.

The best-performing plateau now includes phi0 0.20/phi1 0.80, so the most useful remaining question is whether this perfect method can be accelerated without losing the critical resolution. A 12 min gradient directly tests the faster side of that local optimum and could reveal whether this branch is any more speed-tolerant than the phi0 0.15/phi1 0.85 branch.

For the final shot, test the one untried adjacent corner that could plausibly recover the early pair lost at phi0 0.25/phi1 0.80 while staying near the proven optimum plateau. Raising phi1 to 0.85 at phi0 0.25 keeps the stronger start but steepens the late gradient, which may relieve the early compression enough to map the true upper boundary of the perfect region.
